The princely one, the princely one came forth from the house.
Enlil, the princely one, came forth from the house.
The princely one came forth royally from the house.
Enlil lifted his glance over all the lands, and the lands raised themselves to Enlil.
The four corners of heaven became green for Enlil like a garden.
Keš was positioned there for him with head uplifted, and as Keš lifted its head among all the lands, Enlil spoke the praises of Keš.
with its words she wove it intricately like a net.

Written on tablets it was held in her hands: House, platform of the Land, important fierce bull! House Keš, platform of the Land, important fierce bull! Growing as high as the hills, embracing the heavens, growing as high as E-kur, lifting its head among the mountains! Rooted in the abzu, verdant like the mountains! Will anyone else bring forth something as great as Keš? Will any other mother ever give birth to someone as great as its hero Ašgi? Who has ever seen anyone as great as its lady Nintud?
Thou showest thyself in this land,
Coming in peace, giving life to Egypt:
O Ammon, (thou) leadest night into day,
A leading that rejoices the heart!
Overflowing the gardens created by Ra.
Lover of food, bestower of corn,
Giving light to every home, O Ptah!
Lord of fishes, when the inundation returns
No fowls fall on the cultures.
Maker of spelt; creator of wheat:
For myriads, for all the wretched.
If the gods in heaven are grieved,
He maketh the whole land open to the oxen,
And the great and the small are rejoicing;
The response of men at his coming!
He shineth, then the land exulteth!
Bringer of food! Great lord of provisions!
Lord of terrors and of choicest joys!
He produceth grass for the oxen;
The choice incense is that which he supplies.
He filleth the granaries, enricheth the storehouses,
He careth for the state of the poor.
He causeth growth to fulfil all desires,
He maketh his might a barker,
He is not graven in marble,
As an image bearing the double crown.
He hath neither ministrants nor offerings:
He is not adored in sanctuaries:
No shrine is found with painted figures.
There is no building that can contain him!
There is no counsellor in thy heart!
Thy youth delight in thee, thy children:
Thy law is established in the whole land,
In the presence of thy servants in the North:
Every eye is satisfied with him:
He careth for the abundance of his blessings.
The tooth of the crocodiles, the children of Neith
(Even) the circle of gods who are counted with thee.
Doth not its outburst water the fields,
There is none who worketh with him;
He produces food without the aid of Neith.
He giveth light on his coming from darkness:
In the pastures of his cattle
What was not, his moisture bringeth to life.
Men are clothed to fill his gardens:
He is the infinite Ptah and Kabes.
All his implements in the North.
He enters with words the interior of his house,
When he willeth he goeth forth from his mystic fane.
Thy wrath is destruction of fishes.
Then men implore thee for the waters of the season.
That the Thebaid may be seen like the Delta.
That every man be seen bearing his tools,
No man left behind his comrade!
No adornment for the sons of nobles,
No circle of gods in the night!
The response (of the god) is refreshing water,
With flattering words to worship thee,
Worshipped together with the mighty water!
No fowls fall on the land.
Thy hand is adorned with gold,
As moulded of an ingot of gold,
Corn in its state of germination is not eaten.
The hymn is addressed to thee with the harp;
It is played with a (skilful) hand to thee!
There s a great one adorning the land;
An enlightener, a buckler in front of men,
Loving the increase of all his cattle.
Thou shinest in the city of the King;
Then the householders are satisfied with good things,
The poor man laughs at the lotus.
Every kind of herb for thy children.
All enjoyment is cast on the ground,
O Inundation of Nile, offerings are made to thee:
Great festivals are kept for thee;
Beasts of the field are caught for thee
Pure flames are offered to thee;
Offerings are made to every god,
As they are made unto Nile.
Nile makes for himself chasms in the Thebaid;
Unknown is his name in heaven,
He doth not manifest his form!
Mortals extol (him), and the cycle of gods!
Awe is felt by the terrible ones;
His son is made Lord of all,
Shine forth, shine forth, O Nile! Shine forth!
Giving life to men by his oxen:
Giving life to his oxen by the pastures!
Shine forth in glory, O Nile.

in days of yore, when the necessary things had been brought into manifest existence, in days of yore, when the necessary things had been for the first time properly cared for, when bread had been tasted for the first time in the shrines of the Land, when the ovens of the Land had been made to work, when the heavens had been separated from the earth, when the earth had been delimited from the heavens, when the fame of mankind had been established, when An had taken the heavens for himself, when Enlil had taken the earth for himself, when the nether world had been given to Ereš-kigala as a gift;

when he set sail, when he set sail, when the father set sail for the nether world, when Enki set sail for the nether world — against the king a storm of small hailstones arose, against Enki a storm of large hailstones arose.
The small ones were light hammers, the large ones were like stones from catapults (?).

The keel of Enki's little boat was trembling as if it were being butted by turtles, the waves at the bow of the boat rose to devour the king like wolves and the waves at the stern of the boat were attacking Enki like a lion.

A Hymn of praise of Her-aakhuti, the living one exalted in the Eastern Horizon in his name of Shu who is in the Aten, who liveth for ever and ever, the living and great Aten, he who is in the Set-Festival, the lord of the Circle, the Lord of the Disk, the Lord of heaven, the Lord of earth, the lord of the House of the Aten in Aakhut-Aten, [of] the King of the South and the North, who liveth in Truth, lord of the Two Lands (i.e., Egypt), NEFER-KHEPERU-RA UA-EN-RA, the son of Ra, who liveth in Truth, Lord of Crowns, AAKHUN-ATEN, great in the period of his life, [and of] the great royal woman (or wife) whom he loveth, Lady of the Two Lands, NEFER-NEFERU-ATEN NEFERTITI, who liveth in health and youth for ever and ever.

He (i.e., Ai, a Fan-bearer and the Master of the King's Horse) saith: Thy rising [is] beautiful in the horizon of heaven, O Aten, ordainer of life. Thou dost shoot up in the horizon of the East, thou fillest every land with thy beneficence. Thou art beautiful and great and sparkling, and exalted above every land.. Thy arrows (i.e., rays) envelop (i.e., penetrate) everywhere all the lands which thou hast made.

Thou art as Ra. Thou bringest [them] according to their number, thou subduest them for thy beloved son. Thou thyself art afar off, but thy beams are upon the earth; thou art in their faces, they [admire] thy goings. Thou settest in the horizon of the west, the earth is in darkness, in the form of death. Men lie down in a booth wrapped up in cloths, one eye cannot see its fellow. If all their possessions, which are under their heads, be carried away they perceive it not.

Every lion emergeth from his lair, all the creeping things bite, darkness [is] a warm retreat (?). The land is in silence. He who made them hath set in his horizon. The earth becometh light, thou shootest up in the horizon, shining in the Aten in the day, thou scatterest the darkness. Thou sendest out thine arrows (i.e., rays), the Two Lands make festival, [men] wake up, stand upon their feet, it is thou who raisest them up. [They] wash their members, they take [their apparel]

and array themselves therein, their hands are [stretched out] in praise at thy rising, throughout the land they do their works. Beasts and cattle of all kinds settle down upon the pastures, shrubs and vegetables flourish, the feathered fowl fly about over their marshes, their feathers praising thy Ka (person). All the cattle rise up on their legs, creatures that fly and insects of all kinds

spring into life, when thou risest up on them. The boats drop down and sail up the river, likewise every road openeth (or showeth itself) at thy rising, the fish in the river swim towards thy face, thy beams are in the depths of the Great Green (i.e., the Mediterranean and Red Seas). Thou makest offspring to take form in women, creating seed in men. Thou makest the son to live in the womb of his mother, making him to be quiet that he crieth not; thou art a nurse

in the womb, giving breath to vivify that which he hath made. [When] he droppeth from the womb ... on the day of his birth [he] openeth his mouth in the [ordinary] manner, thou providest his sustenance. The young bird in the egg speaketh in the shell, thou givest breath to him inside it to make him to live. Thou makest for him his mature form so that he can crack the shell [being] inside the egg. He cometh forth from the egg, he chirpeth with all his might, when he hath come forth from it (the egg), he walketh on his two feet. O how many are the things which thou hast made! They are hidden from the face, O thou

One God, like whom there is no other. Thou didst create the earth by thy heart (or will), thou alone existing, men and women, cattle, beasts of every kind that are upon the earth, and that move upon feet (or legs), all the creatures that are in the sky and that fly with their wings, [and] the deserts of Syria and Kesh (Nubia), and the Land of Egypt. Thou settest every person in his place. Thou providest their daily food, every man having the portion allotted to him, [thou] dost compute the duration of his life. Their tongues are different in speech, their characteristics (or forms), and

likewise their skins [in colour], giving distinguishing marks to the dwellers in foreign lands. Thou makest Hapi (the Nile) in the Tuat (Underworld), thou bringest it when thou wishest to make mortals to live, inasmuch as thou hast made them for thyself, their Lord who dost support them to the uttermost, O thou Lord of every land, thou shinest upon them, O ATEN of the day, thou great one of majesty. Thou makest the life of all remote lands. Thou settest a Nile in heaven, which cometh down to them.

It maketh a flood on the mountains like the Great Green Sea, it maketh to be watered their fields in their villages. How beneficent are thy plans, O Lord of Eternity! A Nile in heaven art thou for the dwellers in the foreign lands (or deserts), and for all the beasts of the desert that go upon feet (or legs). Hapi (the Nile) cometh from the Tuat for the land of Egypt. Thy beams nourish every field; thou risest up [and] they live, they germinate for thee. Thou makest the Seasons to develop everything that thou hast made:

The season of Pert (i.e., Nov. 16-March 16) so that they may refresh themselves, and the season Heh (i.e., March 16-Nov. 16) in order to taste thee. 1 Thou hast made the heaven which is remote that thou mayest shine therein and look upon everything that thou hast made. Thy being is one, thou shinest (or, shootest up) among thy creatures as the LIVING ATEN, rising, shining, departing afar off, returning. Thou hast made millions of creations (or, evolutions) from thy one self (viz.) towns and cities, villages, fields, roads and river. Every eye (i.e., all men) beholdeth thee confronting it. Thou art the Aten of the day at its zenith.

At thy departure thine eye ... thou didst create their faces so that thou mightest not see. ... ONE thou didst make ... Thou art in my heart. There is no other who knoweth thee except thy son Nefer-kheperu-Ra Ua-en-Ra. Thou hast made him wise to understand thy plans [and] thy power. The earth came into being by thy hand, even as thou hast created them (i.e., men). Thou risest, they live; thou settest, they die. As for thee, there is duration of life in thy members, life is in thee. [All] eyes [gaze upon]

thy beauties until thou settest, [when] all labours are relinquished. Thou settest in the West, thou risest, making to flourish ... for the King. Every man who [standeth on his] foot, since thou didst lay the foundation of the earth, thou hast raised up for thy son who came forth from thy body, the King of the South and the North, Living in Truth, Lord of Crowns, Aakhun-Aten, great in the duration of his life [and for] the Royal Wife, great of majesty, Lady of the Two Lands, Nefer-neferu-Aten Nefertiti, living [and] young for ever and ever.
That desirable radiance of the god Savitr may we meditate on,
who shall spur on our thoughts. (10)

א֣וֹרוּ מֵר֗וֹז אָמַר֙ מַלְאַ֣ךְ יְהֹוָ֔ה אֹ֥רוּ אָר֖וֹר יֹשְׁבֶ֑יהָ כִּ֤י לֹֽא־בָ֙אוּ֙ לְעֶזְרַ֣ת יְהֹוָ֔ה לְעֶזְרַ֥ת יְהֹוָ֖ה בַּגִּבּוֹרִֽים׃
תְּבֹרַךְ֙ מִנָּשִׁ֔ים יָעֵ֕ל אֵ֖שֶׁת חֶ֣בֶר הַקֵּינִ֑י מִנָּשִׁ֥ים בָּאֹ֖הֶל תְּבֹרָֽךְ׃
מַ֥יִם שָׁאַ֖ל חָלָ֣ב נָתָ֑נָה בְּסֵ֥פֶל אַדִּירִ֖ים הִקְרִ֥יבָה חֶמְאָֽה׃
יָדָהּ֙ לַיָּתֵ֣ד תִּשְׁלַ֔חְנָה וִימִינָ֖הּ לְהַלְמ֣וּת עֲמֵלִ֑ים וְהָלְמָ֤ה סִֽיסְרָא֙ מָחֲקָ֣ה רֹאשׁ֔וֹ וּמָחֲצָ֥ה וְחָלְפָ֖ה רַקָּתֽוֹ׃
בֵּ֣ין רַגְלֶ֔יהָ כָּרַ֥ע נָפַ֖ל שָׁכָ֑ב בֵּ֤ין רַגְלֶ֙יהָ֙ כָּרַ֣ע נָפָ֔ל בַּאֲשֶׁ֣ר כָּרַ֔ע שָׁ֖ם נָפַ֥ל שָׁדֽוּד׃
בְּעַד֩ הַחַלּ֨וֹן נִשְׁקְפָ֧ה וַתְּיַבֵּ֛ב אֵ֥ם סִֽיסְרָ֖א בְּעַ֣ד הָאֶשְׁנָ֑ב מַדּ֗וּעַ בֹּשֵׁ֤שׁ רִכְבּוֹ֙ לָב֔וֹא מַדּ֣וּעַ אֶֽחֱר֔וּ פַּעֲמֵ֖י מַרְכְּבוֹתָֽיו׃
חַכְמ֥וֹת שָׂרוֹתֶ֖יהָ תַּעֲנֶ֑ינָּה אַף־הִ֕יא תָּשִׁ֥יב אֲמָרֶ֖יהָ לָֽהּ׃
הֲלֹ֨א יִמְצְא֜וּ יְחַלְּק֣וּ שָׁלָ֗ל רַ֤חַם רַחֲמָתַ֙יִם֙ לְרֹ֣אשׁ גֶּ֔בֶר שְׁלַ֤ל צְבָעִים֙ לְסִ֣יסְרָ֔א שְׁלַ֥ל צְבָעִ֖ים רִקְמָ֑ה צֶ֥בַע רִקְמָתַ֖יִם לְצַוְּארֵ֥י שָׁלָֽל׃
כֵּ֠ן יֹאבְד֤וּ כׇל־אוֹיְבֶ֙יךָ֙ יְהֹוָ֔ה וְאֹ֣הֲבָ֔יו כְּצֵ֥את הַשֶּׁ֖מֶשׁ בִּגְבֻרָת֑וֹ וַתִּשְׁקֹ֥ט הָאָ֖רֶץ אַרְבָּעִ֥ים שָׁנָֽה׃
Then sang Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day, saying,
Praise ye the LORD for the avenging of Israel, when the people willingly offered themselves.
Hear, O ye kings; give ear, O ye princes; I, even I, will sing unto the LORD; I will sing praise to the LORD God of Israel.
LORD, when thou wentest out of Seir, when thou marchedst out of the field of Edom, the earth trembled, and the heavens dropped, the clouds also dropped water.
The mountains melted from before the LORD, even that Sinai from before the LORD God of Israel.
In the days of Shamgar the son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were unoccupied, and the travellers walked through byways.
The inhabitants of the villages ceased, they ceased in Israel, until that I Deborah arose, that I arose a mother in Israel.
They chose new gods; then was war in the gates: was there a shield or spear seen among forty thousand in Israel?
My heart is toward the governors of Israel, that offered themselves willingly among the people. Bless ye the LORD.
Speak, ye that ride on white asses, ye that sit in judgment, and walk by the way.

They that are delivered from the noise of archers in the places of drawing water, there shall they rehearse the righteous acts of the LORD, even the righteous acts toward the inhabitants of his villages in Israel: then shall the people of the LORD go down to the gates.
Awake, awake, Deborah: awake, awake, utter a song: arise, Barak, and lead thy captivity captive, thou son of Abinoam.
Then he made him that remaineth have dominion over the nobles among the people: the LORD made me have dominion over the mighty.
Out of Ephraim was there a root of them against Amalek; after thee, Benjamin, among thy people; out of Machir came down governors, and out of Zebulun they that handle the pen of the writer.
And the princes of Issachar were with Deborah; even Issachar, and also Barak: he was sent on foot into the valley. For the divisions of Reuben there were great thoughts of heart.
Why abodest thou among the sheepfolds, to hear the bleatings of the flocks? For the divisions of Reuben there were great searchings of heart.
Gilead abode beyond Jordan: and why did Dan remain in ships? Asher continued on the sea shore, and abode in his breaches.
Zebulun and Naphtali were a people that jeoparded their lives unto the death in the high places of the field.
The kings came and fought, then fought the kings of Canaan in Taanach by the waters of Megiddo; they took no gain of money.
They fought from heaven; the stars in their courses fought against Sisera.
The river of Kishon swept them away, that ancient river, the river Kishon. O my soul, thou hast trodden down strength.
Then were the horsehoofs broken by the means of the pransings, the pransings of their mighty ones.
Curse ye Meroz, said the angel of the LORD, curse ye bitterly the inhabitants thereof; because they came not to the help of the LORD, to the help of the LORD against the mighty.
Blessed above women shall Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite be, blessed shall she be above women in the tent.
He asked water, and she gave him milk; she brought forth butter in a lordly dish.
She put her hand to the nail, and her right hand to the workmen's hammer; and with the hammer she smote Sisera, she smote off his head, when she had pierced and stricken through his temples.
At her feet he bowed, he fell, he lay down: at her feet he bowed, he fell: where he bowed, there he fell down dead.
The mother of Sisera looked out at a window, and cried through the lattice, Why is his chariot so long in coming? why tarry the wheels of his chariots?
Her wise ladies answered her, yea, she returned answer to herself,

Have they not sped? have they not divided the prey; to every man a damsel or two; to Sisera a prey of divers colours, a prey of divers colours of needlework, of divers colours of needlework on both sides, meet for the necks of them that take the spoil?
So let all thine enemies perish, O LORD: but let them that love him be as the sun when he goeth forth in his might. And the land had rest forty years.
नासदासीन्नो सदासीत्तदानीं नासीद्रजो नो व्योमा परो यत्।
किमावरीवः कुह कस्य शर्मन्नम्भः किमासीद्गहनं गभीरम्॥१॥
न मृत्युरासीदमृतं न तर्हि न रात्र्या अह्न आसीत्प्रकेतः।
आनीदवातं स्वधया तदेकं तस्माद्धान्यन्न परः किं चनास॥२॥
तम आसीत्तमसा गूळ्हमग्रेऽप्रकेतं सलिलं सर्वमा इदम्।
कामस्तदग्रे समवर्तताधि मनसो रेतः प्रथमं यदासीत्।
सतो बन्धुमसति निरविन्दन् हृदि प्रतीष्या कवयो मनीषा॥४॥
को अद्धा वेद क इह प्र वोचत्कुत आजाता कुत इयं विसृष्टिः।
अर्वाग्देवा अस्य विसर्जनेनाथा को वेद यत आबभूव॥६॥
इयं विसृष्टिर्यत आबभूव यदि वा दधे यदि वा न।
यो अस्याध्यक्षः परमे व्योमन्त्सो अङ्ग वेद यदि वा न वेद॥७॥

Non-being was not, nor was being then; there was no airy space, nor the sky which is beyond.
What stirred? Where? In whose shelter? Was there water, deep, unfathomable? 1
Death was not, nor deathlessness then; there was no sign of night or of day.
That One breathed, windless, by its own power; other than that there was nothing at all beyond. 2
Darkness there was, hidden by darkness, in the beginning; all this was water without a sign.
What was coming to be, covered by emptiness, that One was born by the power of heat. 3
Desire came upon it in the beginning, which was the first seed of mind.
The poets, searching in the heart with insight, found the bond of being in non-being. 4
Their cord was stretched across: was there a below? was there an above?
There were seed-placers, there were powers; own-power below, giving forth above. 5
Who truly knows? Who shall declare it here: from where it was born, from where this creation?
The gods are later than the creation of this; then who knows from where it came into being? 6
This creation, from where it came into being, whether it was set in place or whether not —
he who is its overseer in the highest heaven, he surely knows; or perhaps he does not know. 7
וַתִּתְפַּלֵּ֤ל חַנָּה֙ וַתֹּאמַ֔ר עָלַ֤ץ לִבִּי֙ בַּֽיהֹוָ֔ה רָ֥מָה קַרְנִ֖י בַּֽיהֹוָ֑ה רָ֤חַב פִּי֙ עַל־א֣וֹיְבַ֔י כִּ֥י שָׂמַ֖חְתִּי בִּישׁוּעָתֶֽךָ׃
אֵין־קָד֥וֹשׁ כַּיהֹוָ֖ה כִּ֣י אֵ֣ין בִּלְתֶּ֑ךָ וְאֵ֥ין צ֖וּר כֵּאלֹהֵֽינוּ׃
אַל־תַּרְבּ֤וּ תְדַבְּרוּ֙ גְּבֹהָ֣ה גְבֹהָ֔ה יֵצֵ֥א עָתָ֖ק מִפִּיכֶ֑ם כִּ֣י אֵ֤ל דֵּעוֹת֙ יְהֹוָ֔ה ולא וְל֥וֹ נִתְכְּנ֖וּ עֲלִלֽוֹת׃
קֶ֥שֶׁת גִּבֹּרִ֖ים חַתִּ֑ים וְנִכְשָׁלִ֖ים אָ֥זְרוּ חָֽיִל׃
שְׂבֵעִ֤ים בַּלֶּ֙חֶם֙ נִשְׂכָּ֔רוּ וּרְעֵבִ֖ים חָדֵ֑לּוּ עַד־עֲקָרָה֙ יָלְדָ֣ה שִׁבְעָ֔ה וְרַבַּ֥ת בָּנִ֖ים אֻמְלָֽלָה׃
יְהֹוָ֖ה מֵמִ֣ית וּמְחַיֶּ֑ה מוֹרִ֥יד שְׁא֖וֹל וַיָּֽעַל׃
מֵקִ֨ים מֵעָפָ֜ר דָּ֗ל מֵֽאַשְׁפֹּת֙ יָרִ֣ים אֶבְי֔וֹן לְהוֹשִׁיב֙ עִם־נְדִיבִ֔ים וְכִסֵּ֥א כָב֖וֹד יַנְחִלֵ֑ם כִּ֤י לַֽיהֹוָה֙ מְצֻ֣קֵי אֶ֔רֶץ וַיָּ֥שֶׁת עֲלֵיהֶ֖ם תֵּבֵֽל׃
רַגְלֵ֤י חֲסִידָו֙ יִשְׁמֹ֔ר וּרְשָׁעִ֖ים בַּחֹ֣שֶׁךְ יִדָּ֑מּוּ כִּי־לֹ֥א בְכֹ֖חַ יִגְבַּר־אִֽישׁ׃
יְהֹוָ֞ה יֵחַ֣תּוּ מְרִיבָ֗ו עָלָו֙ בַּשָּׁמַ֣יִם יַרְעֵ֔ם יְהֹוָ֖ה יָדִ֣ין אַפְסֵי־אָ֑רֶץ וְיִתֶּן־עֹ֣ז לְמַלְכּ֔וֹ וְיָרֵ֖ם קֶ֥רֶן מְשִׁיחֽוֹ׃
And Hannah prayed, and said, My heart rejoiceth in the LORD, mine horn is exalted in the LORD: my mouth is enlarged over mine enemies; because I rejoice in thy salvation.
There is none holy as the LORD: for there is none beside thee: neither is there any rock like our God.
Talk no more so exceeding proudly; let not arrogancy come out of your mouth: for the LORD is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed.
The bows of the mighty men are broken, and they that stumbled are girded with strength.
They that were full have hired out themselves for bread; and they that were hungry ceased: so that the barren hath born seven; and she that hath many children is waxed feeble.
The LORD killeth, and maketh alive: he bringeth down to the grave, and bringeth up.
The LORD maketh poor, and maketh rich: he bringeth low, and lifteth up.

He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory: for the pillars of the earth are the LORD's, and he hath set the world upon them.
He will keep the feet of his saints, and the wicked shall be silent in darkness; for by strength shall no man prevail.

The adversaries of the LORD shall be broken to pieces; out of heaven shall he thunder upon them: the LORD shall judge the ends of the earth; and he shall give strength unto his king, and exalt the horn of his anointed.
אָ֣ז יָשִֽׁיר־מֹשֶׁה֩ וּבְנֵ֨י יִשְׂרָאֵ֜ל אֶת־הַשִּׁירָ֤ה הַזֹּאת֙ לַֽיהֹוָ֔ה וַיֹּאמְר֖וּ לֵאמֹ֑ר אָשִׁ֤ירָה לַֽיהֹוָה֙ כִּֽי־גָאֹ֣ה גָּאָ֔ה ס֥וּס וְרֹכְב֖וֹ רָמָ֥ה בַיָּֽם׃
עׇזִּ֤י וְזִמְרָת֙ יָ֔הּ וַֽיְהִי־לִ֖י לִֽישׁוּעָ֑ה זֶ֤ה אֵלִי֙ וְאַנְוֵ֔הוּ אֱלֹהֵ֥י אָבִ֖י וַאֲרֹמְמֶֽנְהוּ׃
מַרְכְּבֹ֥ת פַּרְעֹ֛ה וְחֵיל֖וֹ יָרָ֣ה בַיָּ֑ם וּמִבְחַ֥ר שָֽׁלִשָׁ֖יו טֻבְּע֥וּ בְיַם־סֽוּף׃
יְמִֽינְךָ֣ יְהֹוָ֔ה נֶאְדָּרִ֖י בַּכֹּ֑חַ יְמִֽינְךָ֥ יְהֹוָ֖ה תִּרְעַ֥ץ אוֹיֵֽב׃
וּבְרֹ֥ב גְּאוֹנְךָ֖ תַּהֲרֹ֣ס קָמֶ֑יךָ תְּשַׁלַּח֙ חֲרֹ֣נְךָ֔ יֹאכְלֵ֖מוֹ כַּקַּֽשׁ׃
וּבְר֤וּחַ אַפֶּ֙יךָ֙ נֶ֣עֶרְמוּ מַ֔יִם נִצְּב֥וּ כְמוֹ־נֵ֖ד נֹזְלִ֑ים קָֽפְא֥וּ תְהֹמֹ֖ת בְּלֶב־יָֽם׃
אָמַ֥ר אוֹיֵ֛ב אֶרְדֹּ֥ף אַשִּׂ֖יג אֲחַלֵּ֣ק שָׁלָ֑ל תִּמְלָאֵ֣מוֹ נַפְשִׁ֔י אָרִ֣יק חַרְבִּ֔י תּוֹרִישֵׁ֖מוֹ יָדִֽי׃
נָשַׁ֥פְתָּ בְרוּחֲךָ֖ כִּסָּ֣מוֹ יָ֑ם צָֽלְלוּ֙ כַּֽעוֹפֶ֔רֶת בְּמַ֖יִם אַדִּירִֽים׃
מִֽי־כָמֹ֤כָה בָּֽאֵלִם֙ יְהֹוָ֔ה מִ֥י כָּמֹ֖כָה נֶאְדָּ֣ר בַּקֹּ֑דֶשׁ נוֹרָ֥א תְהִלֹּ֖ת עֹ֥שֵׂה פֶֽלֶא׃
נָחִ֥יתָ בְחַסְדְּךָ֖ עַם־ז֣וּ גָּאָ֑לְתָּ נֵהַ֥לְתָּ בְעׇזְּךָ֖ אֶל־נְוֵ֥ה קׇדְשֶֽׁךָ׃
שָֽׁמְע֥וּ עַמִּ֖ים יִרְגָּז֑וּן חִ֣יל אָחַ֔ז יֹשְׁבֵ֖י פְּלָֽשֶׁת׃
אָ֤ז נִבְהֲלוּ֙ אַלּוּפֵ֣י אֱד֔וֹם אֵילֵ֣י מוֹאָ֔ב יֹֽאחֲזֵ֖מוֹ רָ֑עַד נָמֹ֕גוּ כֹּ֖ל יֹשְׁבֵ֥י כְנָֽעַן׃

Then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song unto the LORD, and spake, saying, I will sing unto the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously: the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea.
The LORD is my strength and song, and he is become my salvation: he is my God, and I will prepare him an habitation; my father's God, and I will exalt him.
The LORD is a man of war: the LORD is his name.
Pharaoh's chariots and his host hath he cast into the sea: his chosen captains also are drowned in the Red sea.
The depths have covered them: they sank into the bottom as a stone.
Thy right hand, O LORD, is become glorious in power: thy right hand, O LORD, hath dashed in pieces the enemy.
And in the greatness of thine excellency thou hast overthrown them that rose up against thee: thou sentest forth thy wrath, which consumed them as stubble.
And with the blast of thy nostrils the waters were gathered together, the floods stood upright as an heap, and the depths were congealed in the heart of the sea.
The enemy said, I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil; my lust shall be satisfied upon them; I will draw my sword, my hand shall destroy them.
Thou didst blow with thy wind, the sea covered them: they sank as lead in the mighty waters.
Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods? who is like thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?
Thou stretchedst out thy right hand, the earth swallowed them.
Thou in thy mercy hast led forth the people which thou hast redeemed: thou hast guided them in thy strength unto thy holy habitation.
The people shall hear, and be afraid: sorrow shall take hold on the inhabitants of Palestina.
Then the dukes of Edom shall be amazed; the mighty men of Moab, trembling shall take hold upon them; all the inhabitants of Canaan shall melt away.
Fear and dread shall fall upon them; by the greatness of thine arm they shall be as still as a stone; till thy people pass over, O LORD, till the people pass over, which thou hast purchased.

Thou shalt bring them in, and plant them in the mountain of thine inheritance, in the place, O LORD, which thou hast made for thee to dwell in, in the Sanctuary, O LORD, which thy hands have established.
The LORD shall reign for ever and ever.
Bless the LORD, O my soul. O LORD my God, thou art very great; thou art clothed with honour and majesty.
Who coverest thyself with light as with a garment: who stretchest out the heavens like a curtain:
Who layeth the beams of his chambers in the waters: who maketh the clouds his chariot: who walketh upon the wings of the wind:
Who maketh his angels spirits; his ministers a flaming fire:
Who laid the foundations of the earth, that it should not be removed for ever.
Thou coveredst it with the deep as with a garment: the waters stood above the mountains.
At thy rebuke they fled; at the voice of thy thunder they hasted away.
They go up by the mountains; they go down by the valleys unto the place which thou hast founded for them.
Thou hast set a bound that they may not pass over; that they turn not again to cover the earth.
He sendeth the springs into the valleys, which run among the hills.
They give drink to every beast of the field: the wild asses quench their thirst.
By them shall the fowls of the heaven have their habitation, which sing among the branches.
He watereth the hills from his chambers: the earth is satisfied with the fruit of thy works.
He causeth the grass to grow for the cattle, and herb for the service of man: that he may bring forth food out of the earth;
And wine that maketh glad the heart of man, and oil to make his face to shine, and bread which strengtheneth man's heart.
The trees of the LORD are full of sap; the cedars of Lebanon, which he hath planted;
Where the birds make their nests: as for the stork, the fir trees are her house.
The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; and the rocks for the conies.
He appointed the moon for seasons: the sun knoweth his going down.
Thou makest darkness, and it is night: wherein all the beasts of the forest do creep forth.
The young lions roar after their prey, and seek their meat from God.
The sun ariseth, they gather themselves together, and lay them down in their dens.
Man goeth forth unto his work and to his labour until the evening.
O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all: the earth is full of thy riches.
So is this great and wide sea, wherein are things creeping innumerable, both small and great beasts.
There go the ships: there is that leviathan, whom thou hast made to play therein.
These wait all upon thee; that thou mayest give them their meat in due season.
That thou givest them they gather: thou openest thine hand, they are filled with good.
Thou hidest thy face, they are troubled: thou takest away their breath, they die, and return to their dust.
Thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created: and thou renewest the face of the earth.
The glory of the LORD shall endure for ever: the LORD shall rejoice in his works.
He looketh on the earth, and it trembleth: he toucheth the hills, and they smoke.
I will sing unto the LORD as long as I live: I will sing praise to my God while I have my being.
My meditation of him shall be sweet: I will be glad in the LORD.
Let the sinners be consumed out of the earth, and let the wicked be no more. Bless thou the LORD, O my soul. Praise ye the LORD.

לְרֵ֙יחַ֙ שְׁמָנֶ֣יךָ טוֹבִ֔ים שֶׁ֖מֶן תּוּרַ֣ק שְׁמֶ֑ךָ עַל־כֵּ֖ן עֲלָמ֥וֹת אֲהֵבֽוּךָ׃
מׇשְׁכֵ֖נִי אַחֲרֶ֣יךָ נָּר֑וּצָה הֱבִיאַ֨נִי הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ חֲדָרָ֗יו נָגִ֤ילָה וְנִשְׂמְחָה֙ בָּ֔ךְ נַזְכִּ֤ירָה דֹדֶ֙יךָ֙ מִיַּ֔יִן מֵישָׁרִ֖ים אֲהֵבֽוּךָ׃
שְׁחוֹרָ֤ה אֲנִי֙ וְֽנָאוָ֔ה בְּנ֖וֹת יְרוּשָׁלָ֑͏ִם כְּאׇהֳלֵ֣י קֵדָ֔ר כִּירִיע֖וֹת שְׁלֹמֹֽה׃
אַל־תִּרְא֙וּנִי֙ שֶׁאֲנִ֣י שְׁחַרְחֹ֔רֶת שֶׁשְּׁזָפַ֖תְנִי הַשָּׁ֑מֶשׁ בְּנֵ֧י אִמִּ֣י נִֽחֲרוּ־בִ֗י שָׂמֻ֙נִי֙ נֹטֵרָ֣ה אֶת־הַכְּרָמִ֔ים כַּרְמִ֥י שֶׁלִּ֖י לֹ֥א נָטָֽרְתִּי׃
הַגִּ֣ידָה לִּ֗י שֶׁ֤אָֽהֲבָה֙ נַפְשִׁ֔י אֵיכָ֣ה תִרְעֶ֔ה אֵיכָ֖ה תַּרְבִּ֣יץ בַּֽצׇּהֳרָ֑יִם שַׁלָּמָ֤ה אֶֽהְיֶה֙ כְּעֹ֣טְיָ֔ה עַ֖ל עֶדְרֵ֥י חֲבֵרֶֽיךָ׃
אִם־לֹ֤א תֵֽדְעִי֙ לָ֔ךְ הַיָּפָ֖ה בַּנָּשִׁ֑ים צְֽאִי־לָ֞ךְ בְּעִקְבֵ֣י הַצֹּ֗אן וּרְעִי֙ אֶת־גְּדִיֹּתַ֔יִךְ עַ֖ל מִשְׁכְּנ֥וֹת הָרֹעִֽים׃
תּוֹרֵ֤י זָהָב֙ נַֽעֲשֶׂה־לָּ֔ךְ עִ֖ם נְקֻדּ֥וֹת הַכָּֽסֶף׃
צְר֨וֹר הַמֹּ֤ר ׀ דּוֹדִי֙ לִ֔י בֵּ֥ין שָׁדַ֖י יָלִֽין׃
אֶשְׁכֹּ֨ל הַכֹּ֤פֶר ׀ דּוֹדִי֙ לִ֔י בְּכַרְמֵ֖י עֵ֥ין גֶּֽדִי׃

הִנְּךָ֨ יָפֶ֤ה דוֹדִי֙ אַ֣ף נָעִ֔ים אַף־עַרְשֵׂ֖נוּ רַעֲנָנָֽה׃
קֹר֤וֹת בָּתֵּ֙ינוּ֙ אֲרָזִ֔ים רחיטנו רַהִיטֵ֖נוּ בְּרוֹתִֽים׃

כְּתַפּ֙וּחַ֙ בַּעֲצֵ֣י הַיַּ֔עַר כֵּ֥ן דּוֹדִ֖י בֵּ֣ין הַבָּנִ֑ים בְּצִלּוֹ֙ חִמַּ֣דְתִּי וְיָשַׁ֔בְתִּי וּפִרְי֖וֹ מָת֥וֹק לְחִכִּֽי׃
הֱבִיאַ֙נִי֙ אֶל־בֵּ֣ית הַיָּ֔יִן וְדִגְל֥וֹ עָלַ֖י אַהֲבָֽה׃
סַמְּכ֙וּנִי֙ בָּאֲשִׁישׁ֔וֹת רַפְּד֖וּנִי בַּתַּפּוּחִ֑ים כִּי־חוֹלַ֥ת אַהֲבָ֖ה אָֽנִי׃
הִשְׁבַּ֨עְתִּי אֶתְכֶ֜ם בְּנ֤וֹת יְרוּשָׁלַ֙͏ִם֙ בִּצְבָא֔וֹת א֖וֹ בְּאַיְל֣וֹת הַשָּׂדֶ֑ה אִם־תָּעִ֧ירוּ ׀ וְֽאִם־תְּע֥וֹרְﬞר֛וּ אֶת־הָאַהֲבָ֖ה עַ֥ד שֶׁתֶּחְפָּֽץ׃
ק֣וֹל דּוֹדִ֔י הִנֵּה־זֶ֖ה בָּ֑א מְדַלֵּג֙ עַל־הֶ֣הָרִ֔ים מְקַפֵּ֖ץ עַל־הַגְּבָעֽוֹת׃
דּוֹמֶ֤ה דוֹדִי֙ לִצְבִ֔י א֖וֹ לְעֹ֣פֶר הָאַיָּלִ֑ים הִנֵּה־זֶ֤ה עוֹמֵד֙ אַחַ֣ר כׇּתְלֵ֔נוּ מַשְׁגִּ֙יחַ֙ מִן־הַֽחַלֹּנ֔וֹת מֵצִ֖יץ מִן־הַחֲרַכִּֽים׃

I am the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys.
As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters.
As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons. I sat down under his shadow with great delight, and his fruit was sweet to my taste.
He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love.

His left hand is under my head, and his right hand doth embrace me.

The voice of my beloved! behold, he cometh leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills.
My beloved is like a roe or a young hart: behold, he standeth behind our wall, he looketh forth at the windows, shewing himself through the lattice.

He of the ear that bears the earring, who has mounted the bull, wearing a pure white moon,
smeared with the ash of the cremation ground of the wilds, the thief who stole my heart,
who gave his grace when, in a day of old, he of the petalled flower bowed down and praised him:
the Lord who dwells in glorious Piramāpuram, is it not he?
Wearing an old tortoise's shell, a young snake and the young tusk of a boar,
seeking alms with a dried skull for his bowl, the thief who stole my heart,
while the great ones, rich in learning and in listening, worship his anklets with their hands and praise him:
the Lord who rides the bull and dwells in Piramāpuram, is it not he?
Wearing a white moon of moonlight on his upright, tawny matted locks where the water spreads,
so that my row of lovely white bangles slips away, the thief who stole my heart,
so that men say, 'This is the one town that was first in the world where towns spread wide':
the Lord who dwells in Piramāpuram, whose name has spread, is it not he?
Not only did he shoot the walled cities that rejoiced in the sky; with a gleaming skull-bowl
he came, glad at heart, seeking alms, the thief who stole my heart;
on his mountain-like chest, rich with the earth-loving snake and koṉṟai flowers,
the Lord who rejoices in the woman and dwells in Piramāpuram, is it not he?
'He has oneness and womanhood, he has matted locks, it is he who rides the bull,' so they say,
and as they speak of him as hard to reach, he settled here, the thief who stole my heart;
so that men say, 'This floated in that one age when the dark sea seized all':
the Lord who dwells in Piramāpuram, which won greatness, is it not he?
Becoming a dancer to songs whose sound is mingled with the Vedas, holding the battle-axe,
so that the row of white bangles on my wrist slips away, the thief who stole my heart;
where the tall, lofty groves, dark and full of fragrance, scatter the rays [?],
the Lord who dwells in Piramāpuram, where the crescent moon mingles, is it not he?
He with the river clasped in his matted locks, he of the fire, swinging the flame, winning splendour [?],
wandering with the snake that clasps his garment, the thief who stole my heart;
in the cool seashore groves ringed by backwaters that clasp the sea, the lovely golden-winged swan
clasps its mate in Piramāpuram: the Lord who dwells there, is it not he?
The shoulders that, glistening with sweat [?], heaved up the mountain, that bred such valour:
he crushed the strength of the king of lofty Laṅkā, the thief who stole my heart;
in this world where sorrow shows itself, whenever the many ages appear,
the Lord who dwells in Piramāpuram, whose name shines, is it not he?
As Māl and he of the cool lotus strove to see the feet and the brow of the Lord,
he stretched out and rose so high that they gave up, the thief who stole my heart;
while the people of the world, the women of bright brow first among them, praise him,
the Lord who dwells in Piramāpuram, which cherishes him, is it not he?
While the Buddhists and the witless Jains speak ill of him behind his back, keeping to no true path,
and speak alike [?], he sought alms through the world, the thief who stole my heart;
so that men say, 'This is a marvel, that he wrapped himself in the hide of the rutting elephant as it reeled':
the Lord who dwells in Piramāpuram, like one who is mad, is it not he?
The sage, master of the Vedas of the hard path, who dwells on the flower of the wide pool—
his Piramāpuram of the great path, and the Lord who dwells there: of him
Ñāṉacampantaṉ, who knows him with a mind set on the one path, has spoken
this Tamil of the holy path; for those who know it well, to be rid of their old deeds becomes easy.
In the month of Mārkaḻi, on this good day when the moon is full,
you who would go to bathe, come! Come, you with fine jewels!
Rich young girls of Āyppāṭi, brimming with wealth!
The son of Nandagopa, fierce in deed with his sharp spear,
the young lion of Yaśodā of the lovely eyes,
dark-bodied, red-eyed, with a face like the radiant moon,
Nārāyaṇa himself will give us the paṟai,
so that the people of the earth may praise us, plunge in and bathe! Ēlōr empāvāy!
Ubi cáritas et amor, Deus ibi est.
Congregávit nos in unum Christi amor.
Et ex corde diligámus nos sincéro.
Ubi cáritas et amor, Deus ibi est.
Simul ergo cum in unum congregámur:
Et in médio nostri sit Christus Deus.
Ubi cáritas et amor, Deus ibi est.
Gáudium, quod est imménsum atque probum.
Where charity and love are, God is there.
The love of Christ has gathered us into one.
Let us rejoice and be glad in Him.
Let us fear and love the living God.
And from a sincere heart let us love one another.
Where charity and love are, God is there.
Therefore, when we are gathered together as one:
Let us take care that we be not divided in mind.
Let malicious quarrels cease, let strife cease.
And in our midst may Christ God be.
Where charity and love are, God is there.
Also, together with the blessed, may we see
Gloriously Your face, O Christ God:
A joy which is immense and pure.
For endless ages of ages. Amen.
मा कुरु धन जन यौवन गर्वं
का मे जननी को मे तातः ।
mā kuru dhana jana yauvana garvaṃ
kā me jananī ko me tātaḥ |
When the appointed time has come and is near,
'ḍukṛñ karaṇe' will not, will not save you. (1)
Fool, give up the thirst for gaining wealth;
make your understanding good, and your mind free of thirst.
Whatever wealth you gain, earned by your own work,
Seeing the weight of a woman's breasts and the region of her navel,
do not fall into the grip of delusion.
This is only a change of flesh, fat and the like:
think on it in your mind again and again. (3)
Water lying on a lotus leaf is very unsteady;
life is like it, exceedingly fickle.
Know that the world is seized by sickness and conceit,
and that all of it is struck down by grief. (4)
As long as you are bent on earning wealth,
so long is your own family fond of you.
Afterwards, when you live on in a worn-out body,
no one at home asks so much as a word of you. (5)
As long as the breath dwells in the body,
so long they ask after your welfare at home.
When the breath has gone and the body has perished,
your wife is afraid of that body. (6)
While a child, one is attached to play;
while a youth, one is attached to young women;
while old, one is attached to worry;
no one is attached to the supreme Brahman. (7)
Who is your beloved? Who is your son?
This worldly round is very strange.
Whose are you? Who are you? From where have you come?
Think on the truth of this, here, brother. (8)
From the company of the good, freedom from attachment;
from freedom from attachment, freedom from delusion;
from freedom from delusion, the unmoving truth;
from the unmoving truth, liberation while still living. (9)
When youth has gone, what stirring of desire?
When the water has dried up, what lake?
When wealth has dwindled, what family?
When the truth is known, what worldly round? (10)
Take no pride in wealth, in people, in youth:
time takes all of it away in the blink of an eye.
Leaving all this, which is made of illusion,
know the state of Brahman and enter it. (11)
Day and night, evening and morning,
winter and spring come back again.
and still the wind of hope does not let go. (12)
In this cluster of twelve verses, in full,
this was told to the grammarian:
the teaching was given by the one skilled in learning,
What is this worry of yours about your beloved and your wealth?
Madman, have you no one to govern you?
In the three worlds the company of the good, and it alone,
becomes the boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence. (13)
One with matted locks, one shaven, one with his hair plucked out,
one who has put on many guises in ochre robes:
though he sees, the fool does not see;
for his belly's sake he has put on many guises. (14)
The limbs have grown weak, the head has turned grey,
the old man goes about holding a stick,
and still he does not let go of the lump of hope. (15)
Fire in front, the sun behind;
at night, the knees drawn up to the chin;
alms in the palm of the hand, a dwelling at the foot of a tree:
and still the noose of hope does not let him go. (16)
One may make the journey to Gangasagar,
without knowledge, in the view of all,
one does not attain liberation even in a hundred births. (17)
Dwelling in temples of the gods or at the foot of trees,
the bare ground for a bed, a deer-skin for clothing,
giving up all possessions and enjoyment:
whom does such detachment not make happy? (18)
Whether delighting in yoga or delighting in pleasure,
whether delighting in company or without company,
he whose mind delights in Brahman
One by whom the Bhagavad Gita has been studied even a little,
by whom a drop of the water of the Ganges has been drunk,
by whom the worship of Murari is performed even once:
with him Yama has no dispute. (20)
lying again in a mother's womb:
here in this worldly round, so hard to cross,
shoreless, save me by your grace, O Murari. (21)
His patched cloak made of rags from the street,
his path free of merit and of sin,
the yogi, his mind fixed in yoga,
delights just like a child or a madman. (22)
Who are you? Who am I? From where has one come?
Who is my mother? Who is my father?
Consider all this to be without substance,
and leave the world, an imagining of dreams. (23)
In you, in me and elsewhere there is one Vishnu;
in vain you are angry with me, impatient.
if you wish soon for the state of Vishnu. (24)
With enemy, friend, son or kinsman
make no effort at quarrel or at peace.
everywhere cast off the ignorance that sees difference. (25)
Leaving desire, anger, greed and delusion,
reflect on the Self: 'Who am I?'
Fools without knowledge of the Self
are cooked, hidden away in hell. (26)
The Gita and the Thousand Names are to be sung;
the form of the Lord of Shri is to be meditated on without end;
the mind is to be led into the company of the good;
and wealth is to be given to the poor. (27)
For pleasure one takes one's enjoyment of women;
afterwards, alas, disease in the body.
Though in the world death is the last refuge,
still one does not give up sinful conduct. (28)
Always consider wealth to be ruin:
truly, there is not a trace of happiness from it.
Those who have wealth fear even their own sons:
everywhere this is the established way. (29)
Control of the breath, withdrawal of the senses,
reflection that tells the lasting from the fleeting,
the practice of meditative absorption joined with recitation:
do these with care, with great care. (30)
Wholly devoted to the lotus feet of the guru,
be free soon of the worldly round.
Thus, by restraint of the senses and the mind,
you will see the god who dwells in your own heart. (31)
foremost in the study of 'ḍukṛñ karaṇe',
was taught by the disciples of the revered Lord Shankara
and had his faculties made pure. (32)
Other than the remembering of his name, any means
we do not see for crossing over worldly existence. (33)

O daughter of the mountain, who gladdens the earth, who delights the universe, praised by Nandi, who dwells on the summit of the great Vindhya mountain, who delights with Vishnu, praised by Indra,
O goddess, consort of the blue-throated one, of the vast family, of many deeds, victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 1

Who showers blessings on the best of gods, who assails the unassailable Durdhara, who endures the foul-faced Durmukha, who delights in joy, who nourishes the three worlds, who pleases Shankara, who steals away sin, who delights in the battle-cry,

who rages at the sons of Danu, who is wrathful at the sons of Diti, who dries up the arrogant, daughter of the ocean, victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 2
O mother of the world, my mother, who loves to dwell in the kadamba grove, who delights in laughter, who stays in your own home on the peak of the lofty Himalaya, crest-jewel of the mountains [?],

sweet as honey, who humbled Madhu and Kaitabha, who shattered Kaitabha, who delights in the round dance, victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 3

O you who cut into a hundred pieces the lord of elephants, his body headless, his trunk hacked away [?]; whose lion, lord of beasts, is fierce in valour, tearing open the temples of the enemy's elephants [?],

who with the rod of your own arm struck down the lord of the warriors, felled in pieces, his head cut off [?], victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 4
O bearer of the irresistible, unaging power [?] raised to slay the enemies maddened by battle, who made the lord of the Pramathas, the great Shiva, foremost in clever counsel, your messenger,

whose mind was death to the envoy [?] of the demons, sinful, evil in wish, evil in purpose, evil in thought, victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 5

O you whose hand grants fearlessness to the wives of enemies and to the best of their heroes who come to you for refuge [?], whose hand holds the spotless trident, laid on the neck of the foe who was a spike in the head of the three worlds,

who made the hot-rayed sun resound with the great sound [?] of the gods' drums beating dumi-dumi, victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 6
O you who by your mere cry of hum drove away Dhumralochana and his hundreds of smoke-grey ones [?], who in battle dried up the creeper [?] of Raktabija sprung from Raktabija's blood,

who delight in the ghosts and goblins sated in the great battle with Shumbha and Nishumbha, Shiva, Shiva [?], victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 7
whose bracelets dance on your limbs, quivering as you cling to the bow at every moment of battle, who struck down the foremost [?] of the warriors loud with their quivers of gold-tawny arrows [?],

who made the fourfold army [?] on the stage of the earth, where troops of many colours clash and young warriors [?] cry out, victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 8
who delight in the dance of the women of the gods, rich in gesture, beaten out as tatatheyi, tatheyi, who delight in songs that play with rhythms, kukutha, kukutha, gadada and the like,

who delight in the sound of the mridanga drum, deep with the ring of dhudhukuta, dhukkuta, dhim-dhim, victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 9

praised by the whole world, intent on the highest praise, with cries of jaya, jaya to be chanted and of victory, victory, you who enchanted the lord of beings with the jingling of your anklets, jhana-jhana, jhinjhimi [?],

O half of the Dancer who danced [?], dancer, actor, leading player [?], who delight in drama staged and in sweet song, victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 10
O flower, flower, good-minded, good-minded [?], endowed with a radiance that charms the good-minded, whose face, resting on night, night, night, is like the moon, maker of night [?],
whose lovely eyes rove like bees, bees, bees, O queen of the bees [?],
victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 11
who delight in the finest of wrestlers, met in the great battle [?], surrounded by a company of Bhil women decked with creepers and jasmine [?],
graceful as the finest young red shoots, blossoming and shining [?], victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 12

O you [who move like] the king of elephants, rutting and wild, thick with the ichor flowing ceaselessly from its temples [?], daughter of the king, the ocean, whose form is the moon, store of beauty, an ornament of the three worlds [?],

O daughter of the king [?], [like] Manmatha who bewitches minds full of longing for fair-toothed women [?], victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 13

whose spotless forehead is adorned with a soft radiance, spotless as a lotus petal, and with the crescent [?], [whose gait is like] a flock of swans moving sweetly in play, the home of every grace and art [?],

on whose crown the bakula flowers and swarms of bees meet, among rings of blue water-lilies crowded with bees, victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 14
lovely-minded one, the sound of the flute in your hand putting to shame the cuckoo's song [?], who go to the mountain bowers made glad by the charming humming of the gathered Pulindas,

whose playground is filled with the good qualities of the great band of Shabara women, born of your own qualities [?], victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 15

whose bright-patterned yellow silk at the hips outshines the moon's light with its rays, whose fine toenails shine like moons, lit by the rays flashing from the crest-jewels of the gods and demons bowing down,

whose breasts, full like the temple-domes of elephants, surpass the peak of the golden mountain [?], victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 16

praised by the one who conquered thousands with a single hand, by the thousand-rayed one, by the thousand-handed one [?], whose son was the deliverer in the battle with Taraka, born to deliver the gods [?],

who delight in Suratha and Samadhi, in their like meditation, meditation upon meditation, and in the well-born [?], victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 17
O home of compassion, he who worships your lotus feet day after day, O auspicious one, O Kamala, who dwell in the lotus, how should he not become a home of Kamala?

As I keep in mind that your feet alone are the highest state, what should not be mine, O auspicious one? Victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 18
He who sprinkles the ground, the stage of your virtues [?], with the waters of the river shining with gold [?], does he not know the joy of embracing the jar-like breasts of Shachi?

Let me make your feet my refuge, the auspicious [feet] where dwell the gods who bow and Vani [?]. Victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 19
Your face, a moon, spotless moon of the moon's spotless race [?], wholly draws one to the shore [?]; is he then turned away by the moon-faced, fair-faced women of Indra's city [?]?

But my thought is this, O you whose wealth is the name of Shiva [?]: what is not done by your grace? Victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 20
O Uma, to me, wretched, you must be kind out of compassion and grace alone; O mother of the world, as you are in your compassion, so you are known, O you who delight [?],
whatever is fitting here, may you accept it; you who take away great torment [?], victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 21
Whoever, still, in deep concentration, with restraint and discipline, recites this hymn of praise day after day,
he is attended by Ramā, supreme Fortune, and his own people, and even his enemies, shall honour him.

Lord, the woman who had fallen into many sins,
perceiving your divinity, taking up the part of a myrrh-bearer,
lamenting, brings you myrrh before your burial.
"Alas!" she says, "for night is upon me, a frenzy of licentiousness,
dark and moonless, the love of sin.
Receive the springs of my tears,
you who by the clouds draw out the water of the sea;
bend to me, to the groanings of my heart,
you who bowed the heavens by your ineffable self-emptying.
I will kiss your spotless feet,
and wipe them again with the locks of my head,
whose footfall Eve in paradise, at evening,
having heard it sound in her ears, hid herself in fear.
The multitudes of my sins and the abysses of your judgements,
who will search them out, saviour of souls, my Saviour?
Do not disregard me, your handmaid, you who have mercy without measure."

Per la doussor c’al cor li vai,
Ai! Tan grans enveya m’en ve
Lo cor de dezirer no·m fon
D’amor, e tan petit en sai,
Car eu d’amar no·m posc tener
Celeis don ja pro non aurai.
Tout m’a mo cor, e tout m’a me,
E se mezeis e tot lo mon;
E can se·m tolc, no·m laisset re
Anc non agui de me poder
Ni no fui meus de l’or’ en sai
Que·m laisset en sos olhs vezer
En un miralh que mout me plai.
Miralhs, pus me mirei en te,
M’an mort li sospir de preon,
Lo bels Narcisus en la fon.
Ja mais en lor no·m fiarai;
Pois vei c’una pro no m’en te
Vas leis que·m destrui e·m cofon,
Totas las dopt’ e las mescre,
Car be sai c’atretals se son.
Ma domna, per qu’e·lh’ o retrai,
Car no vol so c’om deu voler,
E so c’om li deveda, fai.
Et ai be faih co·l fols en pon;
E no sai per que m’esdeve,
Mas car trop puyei contra mon.
(Et eu non o saubi anc mai),
Car cilh qui plus en degr’aver,
No·n a ges, et on la querrai ?
A ! Can mal sembla, qui la ve,
Que ja ses leis non aura be,
Pus ab midons no·m pot valer
Precs ni merces ni·l dreihz qu’eu ai,
Ni a leis no ven a plazer
Qu’eu l’am, ja mais no·lh o dirai.
Aissi·m part de leis e·m recre;
Mort m’a, e per mort li respon,
E vau m’en, pus ilh no·m rete,
Chaitius, en issilh, no sai on.
Tristans, ges no·n auretz de me,
Qu’eu m’en vau, chaitius, no sai on.
De chantar me gic e·m recre,
E de joi e d’amor m’escon.

ah, such great envy comes over me
my heart does not melt from desire.
Alas, I thought I knew so much
of love, and I know so little,
for I cannot keep from loving
her from whom I shall never have any good.
She has taken my heart, and taken me,
and herself and all the world;
and when she took herself from me, she left me nothing
but desire and a longing heart.
I have never had power over myself
nor been my own from the hour
she let me look into her eyes,
into a mirror that pleases me greatly.
Mirror, since I saw myself in you,
sighs from the depths have killed me,
for I lost myself just as
fair Narcissus lost himself in the fountain.
never again will I trust in them;
and just as I used to uphold them,
so now I shall abandon them.
Since I see that not one takes my part
against her who destroys and confounds me,
I fear and distrust them all,
for I know well that they are all alike.
In this my lady shows herself
a woman indeed, and I reproach her for it:
for she does not want what one ought to want,
and what one forbids her, she does.
I have fallen out of favour
and have done just like the fool on the bridge;
and I do not know why this befalls me,
unless because I climbed too high up the mountain.
(and I never knew it till now),

has none at all, and where shall I seek it?
Ah, how little would anyone who sees her think
who will never have any good without her,
she would let die, and not help him.
Since with my lady neither prayers nor pity
nor the right I have can help me,
and it gives her no pleasure
that I love her, I shall never tell her so again.
So I part from her and give up;
she has killed me, and as a dead man I answer her,
and I go away, since she does not keep me,

Tristan, you will have nothing more from me,

In the waters of the ocean of the world's dissolution you held the Veda,
taking on, unwearied, the part of a ship.
Keśava, who took the body of a fish, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (1)
The earth stands on your back, vast beyond measure,
made heaviest by the ring of scars from bearing the earth.
Keśava, who took the form of a tortoise, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (2)
The earth dwells on the tip of your tusk, clinging there,
like the streak of the stain sunk into the moon.
Keśava, who took the form of a boar, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (3)
On your fine lotus hand the nail is a wondrous horn
that has torn the bee that was Hiraṇyakaśipu's body.
Keśava, who took the form of the man-lion, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (4)
With your stride you trick Bali, wondrous dwarf,
purifier of people by the water born from your toenail.
Keśava, who took the form of the dwarf, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (5)
In water made of the blood of kṣatriyas the world, its sin removed,
you bathe, and the burning pain of existence is quenched.
Keśava, who took the form of the lord of the Bhṛgus, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (6)
In battle you scatter to the quarters, pleasing to the guardians of the quarters,
a lovely offering of the heads of the Ten-faced one.
Keśava, who took the body of Rāma, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (7)
On your bright body you wear a garment like a rain cloud,
the colour of the Yamunā, come together in fear of the plough's blow.
Keśava, who took the form of the plough-bearer, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (8)
Ah! you censure the whole of the scripture's rule of sacrifice,
O compassionate heart, that shows the slaughter of animals.
Keśava, who took the body of the Buddha, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (9)
To destroy the hordes of the mlecchas you wield a sword,
Keśava, who took the body of Kalki, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (10)
This noble song spoken by the poet Śrī Jayadeva,
hear it: it gives joy, it gives good, it is the essence of existence.
Keśava, who took forms of ten kinds, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (11)

Is it from remembering neighbours at Dhū Salam
that you have mixed tears flowing from your eye with blood?
Or has the wind blown from the direction of Kāẓima,
and lightning flashed in the darkness from Iḍam?
What ails your eyes, that when you say "hold back" they stream,
and your heart, that when you say "come to your senses" it wanders?
Does the lover think that love can be hidden,
between a flood of tears and a heart on fire?
Were it not for passion you would not shed tears over a ruin,
nor lie sleepless at the mention of the willow and the mountain.
So how can you deny a love,
when the honest witnesses of tears and sickness have testified against you?
Longing has fixed two lines of weeping and wasting
on your cheeks, like the yellow of narcissus and the red of the ʿanam berry.
Yes, the phantom of the one I love came by night and kept me awake;
You who blame me for a chaste love, accept my excuse;
had you been fair, you would not blame.
May my state pass you by: my secret is not hidden
from slanderers, nor is my sickness cut off.
You gave me sincere advice, but I do not hear it;
the lover is deaf to those who reproach.
I even suspected the counsel of grey hair in its reproach,
though grey hair is the furthest of advisers from suspicion.

See! once more the Cross returning,
Heav'n and earth in ashes burning!
O what fear man's bosom rendeth,
When from Heav'n the Judge descendeth,
All before the throne it bringeth!
Death is struck, and nature quaking,
To its Judge an answer making!
When the Judge His seat attaineth,
What shall I, frail man, be pleading,
When the just are mercy needing?
Who dost free salvation send us,
Fount of pity! then befriend us!
Faint and weary Thou hast sought me,
On the Cross of suffering bought me;
Shall such grace be vainly brought me!
Guilty, now I pour my moaning,
All my shame with anguish owning;
Spare, O God, Thy suppliant, groaning!
And to me a hope vouchsafest!
Worthless are my pray'rs and sighing,
Yet, good Lord, in grace complying,
With Thy favor'd sheep, O place me!
Nor among the goats abase me;
But to Thy right hand upraise me.
Doom'd to flames of woe unbounded,
Call me! with Thy saints surrounded.
Low I kneel, with heart submission;
Help me, in my last condition!
Ah! that Day of tears and mourning!
From the dust of earth returning,
Man for judgment must prepare him;
Spare! O God, in mercy, spare him!

Lord of the world, who reigned – before any form was created,
at the time when all was made by his will – then his name was called King,
and after all has come to an end – he alone will reign, awesome,
and he was, and he is, and he will be – in splendour.
And he is one, and there is no second to liken to him or to set beside him –
without beginning, without end, and his are the strength and the dominion,
[without measure, without likeness, without change or exchange,
without joining, without parting, great in strength and might.]
And he is my God, and my redeemer lives, and the rock of my pangs [?] in the [day](time) of trouble,
and he is my banner and my refuge – the portion of my cup on the day I call,
[and he is healer, and he is healing, and he watches, and he is help.]
Into his hand I entrust my spirit, when I sleep and I wake,
and with my spirit, my body – the Lord is with me, and I shall not fear.
[In his sanctuary my soul will rejoice; may he send our anointed one soon,
and then we shall sing in my holy house, Amen, amen! the awesome name:]

Exalted be the living God and praised;
he exists, and there is no time bounding his existence.
One, and there is no oneness like his oneness;
hidden, and there is also no end to his unity.
He has no likeness of a body, and he is not a body;
we cannot set his holiness beside him [?].
Prior to every thing that was created,
first, and there is no beginning to his beginning.
Behold, he is Lord of the world to every creature;
he shows his greatness and his kingship.
The flow of his prophecy he gave to
the men of his treasured portion and his glory.
There has not arisen again in Israel one like Moses,
a prophet who beholds his likeness.
A Torah of truth God gave to his people
by the hand of his prophet, the trusted one of his house.
God will not exchange nor alter
his law, for all ages, for any other.
He watches and knows our secrets;
he sees the end of a thing at its beginning.
He repays a man with kindness according to his deed;
he gives the wicked evil according to his wickedness.
He will send at the end of days our anointed one
to redeem those who wait for the end, his salvation.
The dead God will bring to life in his great kindness;
blessed for ever and ever be the name of his praise.
Deo gratias Anglia redde pro victoria!
Owre kynge went forth to Normandy,
With grace and myzt of chivalry;
The God for hym wrouzt marvelously,
Wherefore Englonde may calle, and cry
Deo gratias Anglia redde pro victoria.
He sette a sege, the sothe for to say,
To Harflue toune with ryal aray;
That toune he wan, and made a fray,
That Fraunce shall rywe tyl domes day.
Then went owre kynge, with alle his oste,
Thorowe Fraunce for all the Frenshe boste;
He spared ‘for’ drede of leste, ne most,
Tyl he come to Agincourt coste.
Than for sothe that knyzt comely
In Agincourt seld he sauzt manly,
Thorow grace of God most myzty
He had bothe the felde, and the victory.
Ther dukys, and erlys, lorde and barone,
Were take, and slayne, and that wel sone,
And some were ledde in to Lundone
With joye, and merthe, and grete renone.
Now gracious God he save owre kynge,
His peple, and all his wel wyllynge,
Gef him gode lyfe, and gode endynge,
That we with merth mowe savely synge
Deo gratias Anglia redde pro victoria.
England, give thanks to God for victory!
Our king went forth to Normandy
with grace and might of chivalry;
God worked marvellously for him there,
wherefore England may call and cry:
England, give thanks to God for victory.
He laid a siege, to tell the truth,
to Harfleur town with royal array;
that town he won, and made a fight
that France shall rue till doomsday.
Then went our king, with all his host,
through France, for all the French boast;
he held back for fear of neither least nor greatest
till he came to the Agincourt coast.
Then, in truth, that comely knight
through the grace of God most mighty
he had both the field and the victory.
There dukes and earls, lord and baron,
were taken and slain, and that right soon,
and some were led into London
with joy and mirth and great renown.
Now gracious God, may he save our king,
his people, and all who wish him well;
give him good life and a good ending,
that we with mirth may safely sing:
England, give thanks to God for victory.

Call him a man of Viṣṇu who knows the pain of others.
He does good to others in their sorrow, and even so lets no pride come into his mind. — Vaiṣṇava 1.
In all the world he bows to everyone; he speaks ill of no one.
He keeps speech, loins and mind steady: blessed, blessed is his mother. — Vaiṣṇava 2.
He looks on all with an equal eye and has given up craving; another's wife is his mother.
His tongue speaks no untruth; he lays no hand on another's wealth. — Vaiṣṇava 3.
Delusion and illusion do not take hold of him; firm detachment is in his mind.
His clap has struck to the name of Rāma; all the places of pilgrimage are in his body. — Vaiṣṇava 4.
He is without greed and without deceit; he has held off desire and anger.
Says Narsaiyo: in seeing him, seventy-one generations of the family were carried across. — Vaiṣṇava 5.

Good people all, this Christmas time,
Consider well and bear in mind
What our good God for us has done
With Mary holy we should pray,
To God with love this Christmas Day
There was a blessed Messiah born.
The night before that happy tide,
The noble virgin and her guide
Were long time seeking up and down
To find a lodging in the town.
But mark how all things came to pass
As was foretold, their refuge all
Was but a humble ox's stall.
Their flocks of lambs and feeding sheep
To whom God's angels did appear
Which put the shepherds in great fear
Prepare and go, the angels said
For there you'll find, this happy morn
A princely Babe, sweet Jesus, born.
With thankful heart and joyful mind
The shepherds went the babe to find
And as God's angel had foretold
They did our Saviour Christ behold
Within a manger He was laid
And by his side the virgin maid
Attending on the Lord of Life
Who came on earth to end all strife.
There were three wise men from afar
And on they wandered night and day
Until they came where Jesus lay
And when they came unto that place
They humbly cast them at His feet
With gifts of gold and incense sweet.

In spring, the flower banquet in the high tower;
the cups going round, with the light falling into them;
through the branches of the thousand-year pines it came out:
that light of old, where is it now?
In autumn, the colour of frost on the camp,
showing the count of the wild geese crying as they pass;
it shone along the swords stood in the ground:
that light of old, where is it now?
Now, the midnight moon over the ruined castle:
its light, unchanged, for whom is it?
What remains on the wall is only kudzu;
what sings in the pines is only the storm.
Above in heaven its light does not change, but
flourishing and withering pass on: the shape of the world.
Is it to mirror this that even now, still,
ah, the midnight moon over the ruined castle?

سارے جہاں سے اچھا ہندوستاں ہمارا
ہم بلبلیں ہیں اس کی، یہ گلستاں ہمارا
غربت میں ہوں اگر ہم، رہتا ہے دل وطن میں
سمجھو وہیں ہمیں بھی دل ہو جہاں ہمارا
پربت وہ سب سے اونچا، ہمسایہ آسماں کا
وہ سنتری ہمارا، وہ پاسباں ہمارا
گودی میں کھیلتی ہیں اس کی ہزاروں ندیاں
گلشن ہے جن کے دم سے رشکِ جناں ہمارا
اے آبِ رودِ گنگا! وہ دن ہیں یاد تجھ کو؟
اترا ترے کنارے جب کارواں ہمارا
مذہب نہیں سکھاتا آپس میں بیر رکھنا
ہندی ہیں ہم، وطن ہے ہندوستاں ہمارا
یونان و مصر و روما سب مٹ گئے جہاں سے
اب تک مگر ہے باقی نام و نشاں ہمارا
کچھ بات ہے کہ ہستی مٹتی نہیں ہماری
صدیوں رہا ہے دشمن دورِ زماں ہمارا
اقبال! کوئی محرم اپنا نہيں جہاں میں
معلوم کیا کسی کو دردِ نہاں ہمارا!

ham bulbuleṉ haiṉ is kī, yih gulistāṉ hamārā
ghurbat meṉ hoṉ agar ham, rahtā hai dil vatan meṉ
samjho vahīṉ hameṉ bhī dil ho jahāṉ hamārā

godī meṉ kheltī haiṉ us kī hazāroṉ nadiyāṉ

ai āb-i rūd-i Gangā! vuh din haiṉ yād tujh ko?

Hindī haiṉ ham, vatan hai Hindūstāṉ hamārā
Yūnān o Misr o Rūmā sab miṭ gaʾe jahāṉ se
ab tak magar hai bāqī nām o nishāṉ hamārā
kuchh bāt hai kih hastī miṭtī nahīṉ hamārī
sadiyoṉ rahā hai dushman daur-i zamāṉ hamārā
Iqbāl! koʾī mahram apnā nahīṉ jahāṉ meṉ
maʿlūm kyā kisī ko dard-i nihāṉ hamārā!
Better than all the world is our Hindustan;
we are its nightingales, it is our garden.
If we are in a foreign land, the heart stays in the homeland:
count us, too, to be there, where our heart is.
That mountain, highest of all, neighbour of the sky,
it is our sentry, it is our guardian.
In its lap play thousands of rivers,
by whose life our garden is the envy of paradise.
O water of the river Ganga! Do you remember those days
when our caravan came down to your bank?
Religion does not teach us to keep enmity among ourselves;
we are of Hind, our homeland is Hindustan.
Greece and Egypt and Rome have all vanished from the world,
but to this day our name and trace remain.
There is something in it, that our being is not wiped out,
though for centuries the turning of time has been our enemy.
Iqbal! We have no confidant in the world:
what does anyone know of our hidden pain!
আমার সোনার বাংলা, আমি তোমায় ভালোবাসি।
চিরদিন তোমার আকাশ, তোমার বাতাস, আমার প্রাণে বাজায় বাঁশি॥
ও মা, ফাগুনে তোর আমের বনে ঘ্রাণে পাগল করে,
ও মা, অঘ্রানে তোর ভরা ক্ষেতে আমি কী দেখেছি মধুর হাসি॥
কী শোভা, কী ছায়া গো, কী স্নেহ, কী মায়া গো—
কী আঁচল বিছায়েছ বটের মূলে, নদীর কূলে কূলে।
মা, তোর মুখের বাণী আমার কানে লাগে সুধার মতো,
মা, তোর বদনখানি মলিন হলে, ও মা, আমি নয়নজলে ভাসি॥
তোমার এই খেলাঘরে শিশুকাল কাটিল রে,
তোমারি ধুলামাটি অঙ্গে মাখি ধন্য জীবন মানি।
তুই দিন ফুরালে সন্ধ্যাকালে কী দীপ জ্বালিস ঘরে,
তখন খেলাধুলা সকল ফেলে, ও মা, তোমার কোলে ছুটে আসি॥
ধেনু-চরা তোমার মাঠে, পারে যাবার খেয়াঘাটে,
সারা দিন পাখি-ডাকা ছায়ায়-ঢাকা তোমার পল্লীবাটে,
তোমার ধানে-ভরা আঙিনাতে জীবনের দিন কাটে,
ও মা, আমার যে ভাই তারা সবাই, ও মা, তোমার রাখাল তোমার চাষি॥
ও মা, তোর চরণেতে দিলেম এই মাথা পেতে–
দে গো তোর পায়ের ধূলা, সে যে আমার মাথার মানিক হবে।
ও মা, গরিবের ধন যা আছে তাই দিব চরণতলে,
আমি পরের ঘরে কিনব না আর, মা, তোর ভূষণ ব’লে গলার ফাঁসি॥
āmāra sonāra bāṁlā, āmi tomāẏa bhālobāsi.
ciradina tomāra ākāśa, tomāra bātāsa, āmāra prāṇe bājāẏa bām̐śi.
o mā, phāgune tora āmera bane ghrāṇe pāgala kare,
o mā, aghrāne tora bharā kṣete āmi kī dekhechi madhura hāsi.
kī śobhā, kī chāẏā go, kī sneha, kī māẏā go—
kī ām̐cala bichāẏecha baṭera mūle, nadīra kūle kūle.
mā, tora mukhera bāṇī āmāra kāne lāge sudhāra mato,
mā, tora badanakhāni malina hale, o mā, āmi naẏanajale bhāsi.
tomāra ei khelāghare śiśukāla kāṭila re,
tomāri dhulāmāṭi aṅge mākhi dhanya jībana māni.
tui dina phurāle sandhyākāle kī dīpa jbālisa ghare,
takhana khelādhulā sakala phele, o mā, tomāra kole chuṭe āsi.
dhenu-carā tomāra māṭhe, pāre yābāra kheẏāghāṭe,
sārā dina pākhi-ḍākā chāẏāẏa-ḍhākā tomāra pallībāṭe,
tomāra dhāne-bharā āṅināte jībanera dina kāṭe,
o mā, āmāra ye bhāi tārā sabāi, o mā, tomāra rākhāla tomāra cāṣi.
o mā, tora caraṇete dilema ei māthā pete–
de go tora pāẏera dhūlā, se ye āmāra māthāra mānika habe.
o mā, garibera dhana yā āche tāi diba caraṇatale,
āmi parera ghare kinaba nā āra, mā, tora bhūṣaṇa ba’le galāra phām̐si.
My golden Bengal, I love you.
Forever your sky, your air play a flute in my heart.
O Mother, in Phalgun the scent of your mango groves drives me mad,
ah, I could die, ah, ah—
O Mother, in Aghran, in your full fields, what a sweet smile I have seen!
What beauty, what shade, what tenderness, what love—
what a sari's end you have spread at the foot of the banyan, along the banks of the rivers!
Mother, the words of your mouth touch my ears like nectar,
ah, I could die, ah, ah—
Mother, when your face grows dim, O Mother, I float in the water of my eyes.
In this playhouse of yours my childhood passed;
smearing your own dust and earth on my limbs, I count my life blessed.
When the day runs out, at evening, what a lamp you light in the house!
Ah, I could die, ah, ah—
then, leaving all my play, O Mother, I come running to your lap.
In your fields where the cattle graze, at the ferry landings for crossing over,
on your village paths loud with birds all day and covered in shade,
in your courtyards full of rice the days of life pass,
ah, I could die, ah, ah—
O Mother, those who are my brothers, all of them, O Mother, are your herdsmen, your farmers.
O Mother, at your feet I have laid down this head—
give me the dust of your feet: it will be the jewel on my head.
O Mother, what wealth the poor have, that I will give at your feet;
ah, I could die, ah, ah—
I will no longer buy in others' houses, Mother, calling it your ornament, a noose for my neck.

এমন ধানের উপর ঢেউ খেলে যায় বাতাস কাহার দেশে!
এমন দেশটি কোথাও খুঁজে পাবে নাকো তুমি,
ও সে সকল দেশের রানি সে যে–আমার জন্মভূমি।
পুষ্পে পুষ্পে ভরা শাখী; কুঞ্জে কুঞ্জে গাহে পাখি;
গুঞ্জরিয়া আসে অলি পুঞ্জে পুঞ্জে ধেয়ে–
তারা, ফুলের উপর ঘুমিয়ে পড়ে ফুলের মধু খেয়ে;
এমন দেশটি কোথাও খুঁজে পাবে নাকো তুমি,
ও সে সকল দেশের রানি সে যে–আমার জন্মভূমি।
ভায়ের মায়ের এত স্নেহ কোথায় গেলে পাবে কেহ!–
ও মা তোমার চরণ দুটি বক্ষে আমার ধরি,

এমন দেশটি কোথাও খুঁজে পাবে নাকো তুমি,

Full of wealth, of grain and flowers, is this earth of ours;
in its midst there is one land—the best of all lands;—
O, it is made of dreams, that land, ringed round with memories;
such a land you will find nowhere, search as you may,
O, she is the queen of all lands—she is the land of my birth.
Moon, sun, planets, stars—where do they shine in such a way?
Where does the lightning play like this, in clouds as black as these!
To the calls of her birds I rise from sleep, waking to the calls of birds;
such a land you will find nowhere, search as you may,
O, she is the queen of all lands—she is the land of my birth.
Whose are rivers so gentle, where are hills so misty!
Where do such green fields melt into the foot of the sky!
In whose land does the wind play like this in waves over the rice!
such a land you will find nowhere, search as you may,
O, she is the queen of all lands—she is the land of my birth.
Trees full of flower upon flower; in bower upon bower the birds sing;
humming, the bees come rushing, swarm upon swarm—
they fall asleep upon the flowers, having drunk the flowers' honey;
such a land you will find nowhere, search as you may,
O, she is the queen of all lands—she is the land of my birth.
Where could anyone go and find such love of brother and of mother!—
O Mother, I hold your two feet to my breast;
my birth was in this land—may I die in this land—
such a land you will find nowhere, search as you may,
O, she is the queen of all lands—she is the land of my birth.

একলা চলো একলা চলো একলা চলো একলা চলো রে॥
যদি কেউ কথা না কয়, ওরে ওরে ও অভাগা,
যদি সবাই থাকে মুখ ফিরায়ে সবাই করে ভয়—
ও তুই মুখ ফুটে তোর মনের কথা একলা বলো রে॥
যদি সবাই ফিরে যায়, ওরে ওরে ও অভাগা,
যদি গহন পথে যাবার কালে কেউ ফিরে না চায়—
ও তুই রক্তমাখা চরণতলে একলা দলো রে॥
যদি আলো না ধরে, ওরে ওরে ও অভাগা,
যদি ঝড়-বাদলে আঁধার রাতে দুয়ার দেয় ঘরে—
আপন বুকের পাঁজর জ্বালিয়ে নিয়ে একলা জ্বলো রে॥

Take Me Out to the Ball Game
Had the fever and had it bad.
Just to root for the home town crew,
On a Saturday her young beau
Called to see if she'd like to go
To see a show, but Miss Kate said "No,
I'll tell you what you can do:"
Take me out to the ball game,
Take me out with the crowd;
Buy me some peanuts and Cracker Jack,
I don't care if I never get back.
Let me root, root, root for the home team
If they don't win, it's a shame.
For it's one, two, three strikes, you're out,
Katie Casey saw all the games,
Knew the players by their first names.
Told the umpire he was wrong,
When the score was just two to two,
Katie Casey knew what to do,
Just to cheer up the boys she knew,
She made the gang sing this song:
We'll sing a song, a soldier's song,
As round our blazing fires we throng,
And as we wait the morning's light,
Here in the silence of the night,
Soldiers are we, whose lives are pledged to Ireland;
Some have come from a land beyond the wave.
Sworn to be free, No more our ancient sire land
Shall shelter the despot or the slave.
Tonight we man the gap of danger
In Erin's cause, come woe or weal
In valley green, on towering crag,
And conquered 'neath the same old flag
We're children of a fighting race,
That never yet has known disgrace,
And as we march, the foe to face,
Sons of the Gael! Men of the Pale!
The long watched day is breaking;
Our camp fires now are burning low;
See in the east a silv'ry glow,
Out yonder waits the Saxon foe,
As we come marching, marching, in the beauty of the day,
A million darkened kitchens, a thousand mill-lofts gray
Are touched with all the radiance that a sudden sun discloses,
For the people hear us singing, "Bread and Roses, Bread and Roses."
As we come marching, marching, we battle, too, for men—
For they are women's children and we mother them again.
Our days shall not be sweated from birth until life closes—
Hearts starve as well as bodies: Give us Bread, but give us Roses.
As we come marching, marching, unnumbered women dead
Go crying through our singing their ancient song of Bread;
Small art and love and beauty their trudging spirits knew—
Yes, it is Bread we fight for—but we fight for Roses, too.
As we come marching, marching, we bring the Greater Days—
The rising of the women means the rising of the race.
No more the drudge and idler—ten that toil where one reposes—
But a sharing of life's glories: Bread and Roses, Bread and Roses.

Thou art the ruler of the minds of all people, dispenser of India's destiny. Thy name rouses the hearts of the Panjaub, Sind, Gujarat and Maratha, of the Dravida and Orissa and Bengal; it echoes in the hills of the Vindhyas and Himalayas, mingles in the music of the Jamuna and Ganges and is chanted by the waves of the Indian Sea. They pray for thy blessings and sing thy praise. The saving of all people waits in thy hand, thou dispenser of India's destiny.

Day and night thy voice goes out from land to land calling the Hindus, Buddhists, Shikhs and Jains round thy throne and the Parsees, Mussalmans and Christians. The East and West join hands in their prayer to thee, and the garland of love is woven. Thou bringest the hearts of all people into the harmony of one life, thou dispenser of India's destiny.

The procession of pilgrims passes over the endless road rugged with the rise and fall of nations; and it resounds with the thunder of thy wheels, Eternal Charioteer! Through the dire days of doom thy trumpet sounds and men are led by thee across death. Thy finger points the path to all people, Oh dispenser of Indias destiny!

The darkness was dense and deep was the night. My country lay in a deathlike silence of swoon. But thy mother arms were round her and thine eyes gazed upon her troubled face in sleepless love through her hours of ghastly dreams. Thou art the companion and the saviour of the people in their sorrows, thou dispenser of India's destiny,

The night fades; the light breaks over the peaks of the Eastern hills; the birds begin to sing and the morning breeze carries the breath of new life. The rays of thy mercy have touched the waking land with their blessings. Victory to the King of Kings, Victory to thee, dispenser of India's destiny.

Do not fear; the crimson banner that waves in these dawns will not fade
before the last hearth that smokes over my homeland is put out.
It is the star of my nation; it will shine;
it is mine, and it belongs to my nation alone.
Do not frown, may I be your sacrifice, O coy crescent,
smile on my heroic race! Why this violence, this wrath?
Otherwise the blood we have shed will not be lawful to you then.
Independence is the right of my nation, which worships God.
I have lived free since time began, and free I live.

I am like a roaring flood; I trample my dam and surge over it;
I tear the mountains, I do not fit into the open expanses, I overflow.
If the horizons of the West are walled in by armour of steel,
I have a frontier like my breast full of faith.
Let it howl, do not fear! How could it strangle such a faith,
Friend, do not let the vile ones reach my homeland, beware;
make your body a shield, let this shameless onslaught stop.
The days that God promised you will dawn;
who knows, perhaps tomorrow; perhaps even sooner than tomorrow.
Do not pass over the ground you tread on, calling it 'soil': know it!
Think of the thousands lying beneath it without a shroud.
You are the son of a martyr. Do not hurt your forefather, it would be a shame;
do not give this paradise of a homeland, even if you were to gain worlds.
Who would not be sacrificed for the sake of this paradise of a homeland?
Martyrs would gush out if you squeezed its soil, martyrs!
Let God take my life, my beloved, all that I have,
but let Him not part me in this world from my only homeland.
O my God, the one wish of my soul from You is this:
let no stranger's hand touch the breast of my temple.
These calls to prayer, whose testimonies are the foundation of the faith,

my corpse will spring from the earth like a disembodied spirit;
then, rising, my head will perhaps touch the Throne.
Wave you too like the dawns, O glorious crescent!
Let all the blood I have shed now be lawful at last.
Forever there is no perishing for you, nor for my race:
freedom is the right of my flag, which has lived free;
independence is the right of my nation, which worships God.

Until the waters of the East Sea and Mount Baekdu dry up and wear away,

Mugunghwa, three thousand ri of splendid rivers and mountains:

The autumn sky is wide and empty, high and without clouds;

With this spirit and this heart, giving all our loyalty,
